subject: physics
title: Binding Lab
summary: Pull a nucleus apart, settle a reaction’s Q value with the right sign and work out the energy a fuel can give.
ncertRef: Section 13.4, Mass-energy and nuclear binding energy
concepts: The Q value of a reaction
learningOutcome: The student can find the binding energy from the mass defect, the Q value of a reaction with its sign, and the energy released by a mass of fission or fusion fuel.

levels.title: Stacker’s tower
levels.adds: Baseline: binding energy = [Z m_H + (A − Z) m_n − m] × 931.5 MeV (Ex 13.1, 13.2; Example 13.3).
hints: Add up Z hydrogen atoms and A − Z neutrons, then subtract the mass of the atom: that is Δm in u.
Convert with 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², so the binding energy is Δm × 931.5 MeV.
Using m_H for the protons accounts for the electrons too, because the masses given are atomic masses.

levels.title: Coin’s trades
levels.adds: New idea: Q = (mass before − mass after) × 931.5 MeV; a negative Q means the reaction needs energy (Ex 13.5, 13.6).
hints: Add the masses on each side and take (before − after).
Convert the difference in u to MeV with 931.5 MeV/u.
A negative Q means energy has to be supplied: the reaction is endothermic, and fission into those pieces is not possible.

levels.title: Plant’s fuel
levels.adds: Apply it: energy = number of events × energy per event, or E = mc² for a mass turned fully into energy (Ex 13.7, 13.8; Example 13.2).
hints: Find the number of atoms: moles × 6.023 × 10²³, with moles = mass in grams ÷ molar mass.
Multiply by the energy per event in MeV, then by 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J per MeV.
For fusion of deuterium, one event uses two deuterons and gives 3.27 MeV.

misconceptions: The mass of a nucleus is the sum of the masses of its protons and neutrons
A reaction that conserves the number of nucleons conserves the total mass too
Energy is released whenever a nucleus splits
